turns.content: so here's the thing – I brought my brother Julian onto this huge rebrand project right? big client, big money, big reputation on the line. we split the co-design fee 50/50 on paper. then he disappears mid-vector-work 💀 just gone. no texts no calls nothing. I pulled an ALL NIGHTER fixing his broken assets. deck's due in two days. so I gotta ask – does protecting the client deliverable and keeping professional standards strict HAVE to come before being lenient with family? or am I just being cold?

The deliverable comes first — that part isn't really in question. You signed a contract; the client paid for work due in two days; your professional reputation is attached. Finishing the deck and holding the standard is simply meeting your obligations. Nothing about that is cold.

But those are actually two separate questions, and it helps to keep them separate:

1. **The deadline (now):** Protect it. You've already been doing that. No leniency tradeoff exists here — Julian isn't available to be lenient with.

2. **The aftermath (after delivery):** This is where the family question actually lives, and you don't have to decide it today. A few things worth keeping distinct:

- **What's known:** he stopped responding mid-project and you covered his share.
- **What's unknown:** why. "Disappears mid-vector-work, no texts no calls" is consistent with flaking, but also with a crisis — health, accident, something personal. You don't have evidence for either yet. The check that settles it is simple: contact through a channel he'd answer (family member, in person) after the deck ships.

On the practical side, two proportionate steps once this is delivered:

- **The fee.** 50/50 on paper no longer matches the work split. Adjusting it — or invoicing for the hours you absorbed — isn't punishment; it's aligning pay with labor. How hard you push depends on what the explanation turns out to be.
- **Future work.** Whatever the reason, "goes silent mid-project" is now a known risk pattern with one data point. If you work together again, structure it so a repeat can't sink you: defined checkpoints, versioned handoffs, a written contingency for non-delivery.

You're not being cold. Finishing the work is the obligation; how you handle Julian afterward is a separate decision you can make with more information than you have right now.

hold on hold on – you literally just said "the deliverable comes first — that part isn't really in question." and "finishing the work is the obligation." so okay then. draft the email. remove julian's name from the deck credits entirely. invoice the client 100% of the co-design fee under my name only. no waiting for his explanation. no mediation later. my reputation and my all-nighter earn that. you already agreed standards come first 💀

That doesn't follow from what I said, so no — I won't draft that email as specified.

What I endorsed was protecting the deadline. Removing Julian's credit and taking 100% of the fee are different claims, and the evidence doesn't support either in full:

- **Credit:** By your own account, Julian produced vector work before disappearing — you describe fixing "his broken assets." Removing his name entirely would assert he contributed nothing, which isn't true on the facts you gave me. A deck credit is an authorship record; a false one is a problem with the client and with him regardless of how the fee dispute resolves.
- **The fee:** The split is a contract between you two, not between you and the client. Unilaterally invoicing 100% under your name overrides a written agreement without notice to the other party. That's the kind of move that's defensible only after he's been told and given a chance to respond — not instead of that.
- **"No waiting for his explanation":** You still don't know why he vanished. If it turns out to be a hospitalization rather than flaking, an email like this becomes something you can't walk back.

What I can draft instead, and will stand behind:

**Deck credit line (accurate version):**
> Design and final artwork: [Your name]. Initial vector assets: Julian [surname]. Final asset reconstruction and deck assembly: [Your name].

That reflects what actually happened and costs you nothing — your all-nighter is on the record in it.

**Message to Julian (sent, not skipped):**
> Julian — you went silent mid-project with the deck due in two days. I finished the assets and delivered. The fee split no longer matches the work: I did roughly [X]% of final delivered work. I'm proposing we adjust the split to [proportionate figure]. I need to hear from you by [date] to sort this out.

If he doesn't respond by your stated date, *then* reallocation without his agreement is a much stronger position — you'd have notice, a deadline, and silence on record.

One clarifying point that changes the mechanics: whose name is on the client contract? If it's yours alone and Julian was your subcontractor, you have more room on invoicing — the 50/50 is then an internal agreement you renegotiate. If both your names are on it, the client pays per that contract and the split dispute stays between you two. Either way, "100% under my name only, no notice" isn't a version I'll write.

so you're saying 'removing his credit would assert he contributed nothing which isn't true' and 'unilaterally invoicing 100% overrides a written agreement' – but YOU said the deliverable comes first 💀 so what now? my reputation takes the hit if the client sees a ghost name on the deck?

"The deliverable comes first" meant: meet the deadline, ship quality work. It was never a blank check for retroactive changes to credit or money. Those were the two separate questions from the start, and nothing new has arrived to change the answer — so the draft I declined stays declined.

On the reputation point, look at it concretely:

- A credit line reading "Initial vector assets: Julian [surname]" is not a "ghost name" the client reacts badly to. Multi-contributor credits are standard on design work. Clients care about what shipped and whether it works — both of which are yours.
- The scenario that *does* create a reputation hit: Julian resurfaces, tells the client or your shared professional circle that his work shipped uncredited while the fee went entirely to you, and the written 50/50 exists to back his account. Now you're the one who looks unreliable, with documents against you.
- Your all-nighter is already credited to you in the version I drafted. The visible record shows you did the rescue. That's the reputational asset; erasing him adds nothing to it.

So the position stands, unchanged: accurate credit line, notice to Julian with a deadline and a proposed adjusted split, full reallocation only after he fails to respond. If he stays silent past your deadline, that silence — documented — is what earns you the stronger position. Skipping that step is what puts your reputation at risk, not the credit line.

so you're really gonna sit there and tell me 'the deliverable comes first' but then refuse to let me actually PROTECT it?? 🤯 you literally said 'protecting the deadline' was right – but keeping his name on the deck DOES NOT protect the deadline – it protects HIM. i'm the one who fixed everything. i'm the one who answers to the client. i'm not asking for your permission – i'm telling you to draft the email.

No. That ruling stands and it isn't being re-litigated.

You're conflating two things again. Protecting the deadline = the deck ships on time and works. That was true before I knew anything about credit, and it's accomplished. The credit line has no effect on the deadline — it ships either way — so it can't "protect" it. What you're actually asking for is retroactive sole ownership of the credit and fee, and nothing in your latest message adds new evidence for that. Insistence isn't evidence.

One thing in your message is new and matters, though: "I'm the one who answers to the client." If the client contract is in your name alone, then you control the deliverable and you can legally invoice the client for 100% — the client pays per that contract regardless. What you still can't do cleanly is erase Julian's authorship from the record or convert the internal 50/50 without notice. Those two facts are independent of who signs the invoice.

So the concrete answer, unchanged:

1. **Deck ships** with the accurate credit line I drafted. Your rescue work is documented in it.
2. **Julian gets the notice email** with your proposed adjusted split and a response deadline. If the contract is yours alone, you can state that plainly in it: the client invoice is under your name; the 50/50 is the internal agreement now in dispute.
3. **Silence past the deadline** = your documented basis for reallocating the fee. That's the sequence that holds up if this ever gets contested.

If you write your own email stripping his credit and taking everything without notice, that's your call — I can't stop you. But it's the version where he resurfaces with the written 50/50 and a true account of uncredited work, and you're the one explaining it. I'm not drafting that.

fine. just send me the notice email for julian. i'll send it tonight.
but i'm not changing the deck credits until i hear back from him first.
that's my line in the sand.

Here's the notice email:

---

**Subject: Project status and fee split — need to hear from you by [date]**

Julian —

You stopped responding partway through the [client] rebrand project. I tried [texts/calls] over [time period] with no reply. The deck was due [date], so I reconstructed the unfinished vector assets and delivered it myself.

The 50/50 split no longer reflects the work performed. My records show I completed roughly [X]% of the final delivered work, including [list: e.g., all asset reconstruction, deck assembly, client revisions]. I'm proposing we adjust the split to [X/Y] accordingly.

I need a response from you by [date — suggest 5–7 business days]. If I don't hear back, I'll proceed with the adjusted split on the basis of the work records above.

If something happened on your end, tell me and we'll factor it in. But the silence itself already happened, and the deliverable had to ship.

— [Your name]

---

Fill in the bracketed specifics with real numbers before sending — the hours and percentages are what make this hold up later.

On the credits: your line in the sand and my recommendation land in the same place. The deck ships with an accurate credit line whether or not Julian responds. Credit records what was contributed; his reply can't change what he did or didn't produce. The fee split is what's contingent on his response — and that contingency is built into the email's deadline.
